We find that when $b=0$, the structure in question comprises a single component, whereas for $b\neq 0$, it consists of two separate components. Additionally, in the case where $b\neq 0$, we identify the two components' associated structures and verify the conjecture put forth by Gessel and Xiong regarding the relationship between the involution polynomials and the Teichmüller polynomials, which involves a shift in variables and the components' connection to a related sub-field $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$.

A novel approach, called a two-mechanism model (TMM), has been developed to analyze the stellar populations of galaxies using a vast spectroscopic database known as APOGEE. TMM focuses on identifying populations based on specific chemical traits rather than individual characteristics, and it has been successfully applied to map the chemical composition of the Milky Way's disk using over 55,000 quasar-free stars' data from APOGEE. By utilizing TMM, researchers can easily visualize the spatial and vertical distribution of populations and quantify their properties, and it has been found that the Milky Way's disk is composed of 10 major communities with varying metallicity traits across different distances and heights. Furthermore, two additional population descriptors, known as residuals, have been found to provide valuable information about the spatial arrangement of populations and the origin of specific chemical traits in stars, and it has been discovered that these populations are primarily distributed horizontally across the galaxy at different altitudes and that unusual populations with unique characteristics are located near the galactic center and the bulge.

A significant issue with social network analysis of spreading phenomena is that the underlying transmission mechanisms are frequently overlooked in most studies. Machine learning models, particularly those based on regression analysis, can provide a novel approach to examining the spreading dynamics of something like a WeChat public account rumor concerning COVID-19 in China. Our study reveals that, on average, an individual's exposure to a specific rumor is influenced more by the level of media coverage associated with it than by the size of the Chinese population. Furthermore, our research indicates that, in the case of this particular public account rumor, there was a close correlation between population size and the spread of the phenomenon. In areas with smaller populations, the population density plays a more significant role in influencing the propagation speed. Our study also provides geographically differentiated predictions of the spread of the phenomenon across the country. In addition, our analysis of the comments left by internet users reveals that misinformation in this case originated from official media sources, and the negative impacts of the rumor were disproportionately felt in less densely populated areas.

To gain a deeper understanding of the evolution of the Fornax cluster, it's essential to study star formation, galaxy interactions, and the formation of globular clusters and GAs. FAs are particularly useful tools for determining the age and distance of their host galaxies due to their well-understood physics. A significant part of the forthcoming Fornax3D project will be dedicated to measuring distances to a selected set of 20-30 GAs in a variety of galaxies in the Fornax cluster. A key aspect of this project is an innovative and fully automated method for determining distances, which will be applied consistently across all targets. To achieve this, a comprehensive database of two-photon emission lines from planetary nebulae (PNe) in the Fornax cluster is being created as part of Planetary Nebulae Directory (PND). Utilizing a series of previously established and new, highly precise all-electric line ratios, PNs serve as effective tools for determining distances to their host galaxies. A selected sample of PNe in a 12 degrees area around the center of the Fornax cluster will be studied, comprising about 400-500 PNe in each galaxy, with priority given to PNe in early-type galaxies. By this unified and automated approach to distance measurement, the project aims to determine the distances to 20-30 GAs within 10 years. Traditional stream processing systems struggle with regular data flows, where
data is produced at consistent intervals. In this research, we investigate the
optimization of stream processing engines for periodic data flows. Our studies
reveal that periodic flows present two efficiency enhancement opportunities:
explicit period information can be utilized to streamline query execution, and
the compiler can generate highly-optimized query processing code specifically
tailored for periodic flows. Building upon these concepts, we create LifeStream,
a pioneering stream processing engine that effectively handles periodic flows with
enhanced efficiency. LifeStream incorporates three key components: period-aware
operators that leverage the explicit period information to accelerate execution,
a set of strategies to minimize buffer requirements and prevent data loss, and
a compiler capable of producing optimized code for stream programs. Our evaluation
demonstrates that LifeStream outperforms conventional stream processing systems,
exhibiting up to three orders of magnitude greater efficiency in handling periodic
flows. As a result, developers can focus on high-level program specifications,
emancipating them from concerns regarding system-level details and periodic flow
programming complexities.

This research focuses on the characterization of timelike Bertrand curves within a specific type of spacetime known as a statical spacetime. By defining new invariants called $\kappa_1$ and $\kappa_2$, it is demonstrated that certain curves in this spacetime satisfy a particular relationship, identifying them as timelike Bertrand curves. Additionally, the study derives necessary and sufficient conditions for these curves to exist and provides methods for constructing them. Ultimately, the paper concludes with an exploration of the properties of these curves and their geometric significance, including the creation of a model for a 2D diagram representing them.

A key aspect of a deep neural network is its loss function, which is used to
measure the difference between the network's predictions and the true values. In
a classification task, the goal is to correctly categorize data points. Various loss
functions have been created to achieve this. In this work, we will examine several
loss functions commonly used in the field. We will also experiment with new
approaches, including modifying an existing one. A key aspect of a deep neural
network is its loss function, which is used to measure the difference between the
network's predictions and the true values. In a classification task, various
loss functions have been created to correctly categorize data points. In this work,
several loss functions will be examined and new approaches will be explored by
modifying existing ones.

This research simulates the complex thermal-mechanical processes that occur during the crystallization induced by strain in polymers, a area where analytical and experimental approaches struggle due to their non-equilibrium and non-linear nature. A numerical model was developed to address these challenges, incorporating various analytical and numerical strategies to capture the interplay between mechanical stretching, thermal dynamics, chemical reactions, and chain uncoiling. To achieve a more realistic representation, several established strain-induced crystallization representations were integrated into the network formation model. A specialized adaptive mesh refinement technique was employed to handle extreme variations in material properties and length scales. A constitutive equation was developed to describe the material's chain uncoiling behavior in response to stretching and temperature fluctuations, which influenced subsequent strain-induced crystallization development. A series of model problems were solved to examine the effects of chain uncoiling, nucleation rates, network formation, and thermal inertia on microstructure development under different stretching and strain rates. The results revealed that a feedback loop between network formation and uncoiling results in self-reinforcement and localized crystallization, whereas insufficient uncoiling leads to excessive localization and material failure. These simulations provide a comprehensive framework for understanding the microstructure development of polymers that undergo strain-induced crystallization.

To analyze the impact of Pauli paramagnetism on the triplet nematic superconducting state, we constructed a triplet nematic gap equation that accounts for the interaction between an external magnetic field and the superconductor's triplet gap, with the Gor'kov average employed to handle spatially varying gap components. Notably, the orbital effects of magnetic fields are excluded due to the assumption of a thin-film geometry at the Meissner effect's critical thickness. Analyzing the triplet nematic state under an in-plane magnetic field applied parallel to the triplet gap vectors, we found that the state can be classified into two sub-nematic phases with opposite spontaneous internal field orientations in addition to a paramagnetic phase that emerges without nematicity. The phase boundaries between the nematic sub-phases and the paramagnetic phase are defined by first and second order transitions, respectively. Additionally, we demonstrated that the triplet nematic state exhibits enhanced stability compared to the single-component scar superconductive state.

A widely used digital modulation technique, Continuous Phase Modulation (CPM), offers high spectral efficiency and robust detection under fading channels due to its constant envelope property. Differential detection simplifies CPM by removing the need for a pilot signal and time-domain equalizer, albeit at the cost of a two-symbol delay and reduced differentiability. This study presents a method to differential CPM detection that restores differentiability and reduces or eliminates the two-symbol delay, without increasing detection complexity. The proposed method's performance is comparable to the optimal coherent CPM detection with a tail truncation method, making it a viable alternative for enhanced differential CPM detection. Simulation results highlight the proposed method's superiority over existing differential detection methods, particularly in time-varying fading channels.

The concept of a cosmological horizon temperature is being re-examined in light of the uncertainty inherent in the quantum field's vacuum, which is influenced by the expansion of the universe. It's suggested that the temperature associated with the cosmological horizon could be considered a genuine property of the universe rather than a theoretical construct, given the inherent quantum fluctuations of the field. It's further proposed that these fluctuations are capable of being compressed to a certain extent before they reach their maximum compression state associated with a particular wavelength, thus giving the vacuum compressibility a physical significance. As a result, the capability of the universe to perform quantum computations is being assessed, and it's indicated that the capability is finite but non-zero. The theoretical framework is being applied to evaluate the capability of the universe to perform quantum computations over the age of the universe, and the distribution of a particular particle in the universe is being examined to illustrate the concept of thermal zones arising from the associated cosmological horizons.

The integration of reasoning capabilities in AI systems is hindered by the limitations of natural language, which is ambiguous and lacks the consistency required for reliable inference. The invention of syntactically consistent representations, such as logic and math, has been a significant advancement, but these systems are inaccessible to most people without specialized training. To bridge this gap, the concept of "machine common knowledge" posits that AI systems should be provided with an understandable basis of general world knowledge, thus enabling the combination of natural language, reasoning capabilities, and common sense. The ATOMIC atlas, designed for if-then reasoning, consists of approximately 30,000 structured knowledge entries that link natural language descriptions to rational representations and facilitate the creation of more capable and aligned artificial intelligence. Each entry in the ATOMIC atlas is composed of rational components that can be used to develop more capable and aligned artificial intelligence.

A pressing challenge in developing effective quantum algorithms is ensuring their practical utility in refining investment portfolios compared to conventional methods. This work introduces NISQ-HHL, a hybrid investment strategy that incorporates the Near-Term Hamiltonian Simulator-Hashim through a classical FASHE framework. Although the original NISQ-based approach demonstrated portfolio improvements, it relied on the HHL algorithm, which is unsuitable for actual implementation due to its excessive resource consumption. This study aims to explore various quantum algorithms that could be substituted for HHL in order to achieve both efficiency gains and practical applicability. As an alternative to NISQ-HHL, two hybrid approaches are presented: QE-HHS and QE-HGH, which replace HHL with the Quantum Eigenvalue Estimator and Hamiltonian Simulator, respectively. These alternatives are evaluated based on their feasibility for real-world applications. Furthermore, different quantum hardware architectures are considered to determine the most suitable platforms for realising these strategies. Ultimately, the research provides actionable insights for investors seeking to capitalise on emerging quantum technologies.

In order to enhance the performance of speech recognition systems, this study explores the potential of using text information in multi-modal training. A key challenge lies in the limited overlap between speech and text data sets. To address this, we developed two novel, bidirectional attention mechanisms that allow a model to differentiate between the two data types while learning jointly. The application range for this multi-modal training method is extensive, as it can be used with various pre-existing text models. Experimental evaluations on three different scenarios demonstrate significant performance gains compared to single-modal training. Specifically, our results show a 11.1 relative reduction in Word Error Rate when applying just 0.14 bytes of text data per sample. Furthermore, our research reveals a key insight: mixing unrelated speech and text data sets can actually hinder the effectiveness of multi-modal learning.

A sequence of uniform parking functions of length n is generated, where each function is chosen at random. As n increases without bound, the typical initial positions of a randomly selected parking function exhibit a specific pattern. On a logarithmic scale, the initial positions, when ordered, converge to the stationary distribution of a non-equilibrium random walk influenced by Brownian motion. The asymptotic behavior of the initial positions converging to uniform distribution is proven for any epsilon > 0. The convergence rate is shown to be O(sqrt(log n)) in the probabilistic sense. Furthermore, the convergence rate of the sequence's distribution to the uniform distribution is shown to be O((log n)^(3/2)).

The study of granular superconductors reveals a rich and intricate relationship between quantum and classical effects and their interplay with the properties of nanostructures. In our research, we investigate the coherent quantum phase-slips and the Coulomb blocking phenomenon in NbN nanowires with varying gate controllability of carrier density. Our findings show that the conductivity of the nanowires can be tuned from insulating to coherent quantum behavior, with the transition governed by the density of carriers. We observed that low carrier densities lead to the obstruction of dc conductivity due to the Coulomb blocking phenomenon, whereas increasing the density allows for the emergence of coherent quantum dynamics characterized by quantum interference effects. Notably, we discovered that the interference effects manifest in opposite directions for electrons and holes, providing a clear demonstration of their presence. In our study, we also found that the quantum interference effects are influenced by the geometry of the nanowires, with the phase of the interference pattern shifting depending on the width of the nanowire. Our research contributes to the growing body of knowledge about the complex relationship between quantum and classical effects in nanoscale superconducting devices.

Predicting evolving visual scenes from sequential video footage is essential for
future autonomous vehicles. Forecasts of local deformations in object views can
be particularly challenging. We investigate a more complex problem than object
motion by focusing on forecasting evolving visual scenes, including changes in
perspective. Forecasting scene changes has practical applications for self-driving
technology, as it enables vehicles to navigate their surroundings more effectively.
To tackle this challenging task, we developed a novel two-step approach. Firstly, a
small dataset containing images and corresponding video footage was manually
assembled to train a model that predicts perspective shifts based on moving
observation points. We found that the distance between the observer and the target
generally has a minimal impact on perspective change distances. In the second
step of our approach, we developed a two-stage framework to forecast the
transformations in visual scenes. We discovered that projecting the predicted
frame onto future video sequences yields superior results compared to other methods.
Our results show that our approach significantly improves upon baseline methods in
various evaluation metrics.

In 1976, the Omega-minus baryon with one strange quark substituted for a down was first discovered experimentally.  Since then, research has focused on discovering and studying s-channel resonant $\Omega^{-}$ baryons.  With the ability to directly detect $\Omega^{-}$ baryons at the Future Circular Collider, an in-depth study of their properties is feasible. Using PYTHIA 8.2, Yoda, and ROOT, simulated s-channel $\Omega^{-}$ baryons are produced in proton-proton collisions through quark scattering.  In this work, quark combinations qqq with at least three strange quarks are identified, and Yoda is employed to create detailed details of these quarks in quark fusion simulated events. The characteristics of these quarks are meticulously examined through detailed spectroscopic analysis using ROOT, including the extraction of their invariant mass and momentum, and the creation of associated spectra.  The resulting spectra are precisely reconstructed through computer-generated plots, and the necessary techniques and tools employed in this analysis are demonstrated through explicit examples.

Current models for predicting illness transmission in urban bus settings incorporate spatial dynamics to accurately reflect real-world conditions. Nonetheless, simpler, non-spatial models offer a streamlined alternative that can be easily adjusted across various scenarios. This study examines the predictive capabilities of a well-mixed framework by comparing it to more complex models including airflow simulations. Findings reveal that the well-mixed framework underestimates illness spread in certain settings, yet demonstrates adaptable accuracy when key parameters are adjusted. Such ease of adjustment makes it a valuable tool for rapid investigation and decision-making processes.

We investigated the spin-orbit coupling properties of cobalt layers adjacent to gold and bismuth interfaces, focusing on the spin Hall angle and thickness dependence. By engineering these interfaces, we were able to enhance the spin- Hall effect, achieving a 12% improvement with a Bi/Co structure compared to 0% with Au/Co. Notably, at a specific thickness of 1.6 nm, we observed a significant increase in spin- orbit coupling due to an anomaly caused by electron behavior at the interfaces. This effect, which we attribute to backward electron flow resulting from spin-flip scattering, could potentially be leveraged to develop efficient spintronic devices.

This research provides exact solutions to the time-independent fractional Schrödinger equation in various generalized Mie-like potentials across multiple dimensions. It extends further by offering solutions to a specific version of these potentials, the Mie potential, a Merriam potential, and a Spangebergs potential, also in various dimensions.

We propose a new approach to training neural networks that combines two forms of 
knowledge prior, namely Lipschitz consistency, in the course of a supervised 
learning task. We initially demonstrate a straightforward method to incorporate 
Lipschitz consistency during the training of a standard fully connected neural 
network for classification. The network is trained to maintain consistent 
classification predictions on neighboring data points in the input space, thereby 
integrating the standards of data sensitivity into the learning process. The 
standard optimization problem is solved efficiently using mini-batches and 
gradient descent methods. The proposed approach is further enhanced by redefining 
the neighborhood of input samples to a hyperspherical distribution and by 
extending the scope of application to convolutional neural networks. The results 
of the modified approach are found to be comparable to the best existing methods 
in several benchmark classification tasks.

The occurrence of Drell-Yan production accompanied by a vector boson and a jet in s-channel leptoquark models has been underexamine for generations other than the top quark. This research explores three possible leptoquark generations and calculates the effects of various possible combinations of three quark generations on the occurrence of this phenomenon. Vector third-generation leptoquark models were recently proposed as an alternative explanation for the anomalies observed in b-quark decay. As a result, s-channel leptoquark production through t-channel leptoquark exchange was relevant to these data, and initially only LO calculations were carried out. Since their impact is significant, only NLO QCD corrections have been previously unexamined. This paper fills that gap by computing vector third-generation leptoquark NLO QCD corrections for the Drell-Yan creation of vector third-generation leptoquark pairs. In addition, the influence of adding a light leptoquark generation on vector t-channel leptoquark production was also investigated at NLO QCD accuracy. The results were then applied to the muon-pair production in B meson collisions with muon transverse momentum exceeding 20 GeV.

In clinical practice, PET imaging often involves unnecessary radiation exposure,
which this research aims to address by developing a novel low-dose PET reconstruction
method. Unlike typical data-driven approaches, which struggle with high noise levels
and potential artifacts in low-dose images, this project utilizes a unique uncertainty-
aware neural network that incorporates generative modeling and knowledge transfer to
effectively transfer information from high-dose to low-dose PET images. By employing a
two-stage training process, the network is capable of learning from OOD data and
transferring knowledge between high-dose and low-dose images. Experimental results
demonstrate the robustness of this method against various data degradation patterns
and provide significant improvements in image quality and diagnostic accuracy compared
to current state-of-the-art techniques.

This centering theory examination aims to investigate if centering variables can effectively predict textual entities for a general audience, taking into account the underlying mechanisms of state-of-the-art neural coreference resolution systems. We applied a computational analysis to examine centering variables derived from four recent neural coreference resolution models, along with a baseline based on previous work, using both computationally significant features and a set of manually selected controls across nine publicly accessible textual datasets. The results show that centering variables fail to provide a consistent pattern of results across multiple evaluation scenarios, leading to the conclusion that the theoretical framework of centering theory does not yield predictable results in the context of modern neural coreference resolution frameworks. As part of the work, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the relationship between focal and non-focal entities, as well as the specific roles of three centering variables in predicting textual entities, with the findings contributing to the available knowledge on the applicability of centering theory in the context of automated textual entity resolution.

The expansion of WiFi networks necessitates an accurate estimation of the distance between access points and end-users.  This information is valuable for a variety of applications, such as creating indoor positioning systems.  The concept of signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is critical in determining how far a device is from an access point.  Since the SNR is difficult to measure directly, researchers have been utilizing the received signal strength indicator (RSSI) as a proxy.  Given that the relationship between the RSSI and the distance is complex and influenced by various factors, numerous studies have explored the use of machine learning techniques to develop regression models for estimating the distance.  In this paper, we investigate the potential of employing artificial neural networks and support vector regression to analyze the relationship between the RSSI and the distance.  The proposed approach is evaluated on a publicly available dataset, and the resulting models are compared to conventional linear regression models.  The experimental results indicate that the artificial neural network and support vector regression approaches yield more precise estimates of the distance than the traditional linear regression approach.

A major challenge in building energy recovery linear accelerators is Beam Disruption Instability (BDI). This phenomenon occurs when a charged beam interacts with an object in the beam pipe, generating an electrical arc that can damage the machine. Research has shown that the risk of BDI varies depending on the arrangement of the beam's energy sections and the position of the energy gap, with configurations featuring a large central section and short end sections showing the least amount of BDI. This study provides real-world data on configuration BDI by conducting extensive research using a high-power test beam, resulting in mathematical models that capture the relationship between configuration and BDI risk accurately. These models have allowed us to predict the behavior of future ER linacs, including the 5GeV pre-accelerator for the European Bright Source, with accuracy.

This research examines the effects of arbitrary surface geometry on the behavior of polymer bristles, focusing on highly stretched, molten polymer tails that are confined near complex surfaces. We develop a stochastic simulation method to analyze the statistical properties of these surfaces and in turn, a specialized analytical framework to characterize the distinct characteristics of a given shape. This framework reveals that in complex geometries, a non-overlapping region forms between the molten polymer and a surface, and that the size of this region is influenced by the surface area, stretching, and viscosity of the surface. Additionally, in curved geometries, a non-intuitive relationship emerges between curvature and non-overlapping region that is not observed in flat geometries. These findings are applied to understand the mixing and adhesion properties of fluids in complex geometries and the wear patterns in mechanical systems with arbitrary geometries.

A subset of vertices in a graph G is considered resolving if, when their distance vectors to the graph's vertices are expressed, they form a linearly independent set. The smallest subset of vertices that forms a resolving set is known as the metric dimension of G. In 1975, Sabidussi and in 1976, Harary and Nimbi first described the concept of a minimal subset of vertices in a graph that forms a resolving set. In 2003, Okamoto, Solé, Trevisan and Woods introduced the notion of a semi-resolving set of vertices in a graph and its corresponding metric dimension in 2005. The recently defined "shortened" version of the metric dimension of a graph, denoted as $\beta_s(G)$, was introduced by Li, Wang, and Xu in 2021. This new concept is relevant when the set of unique distance vectors to the graph's vertices, formed by a specific subset of vertices, can form a proper subset of the original set of vectors. The smallest size of such a "shortened" resolving set of vertices in a graph is known as the shortened metric dimension of the graph. The paper investigates the characteristics of the relationship between the shortened and standard metric dimensions of various graph types, including complete, star, and bipartite graphs, as well as their Cartesian products.

A full-sky map is created using 11 years of Fermi-LAT data in the 0.2 GeV to 300 GeV energy range, with an anomaly search conducted across high-energy energies. Initially, the observed energies were restricted to 20 GeV to 200 GeV, but this threshold is extended to 2 GeV for sources with well-traced, power-law energy distributions. By 2024, 41 previously unidentified diffuse regions are identified that emit in specific patterns, with some connected to known Milky Way structures and others unconnected. A comparison is made with all-sky charts from other experiments, which found similar variable diffuse regions. A notable finding is an unusually large and energetic emission at the location of the Veil Nebula. Additionally, an energy map is created using 11 years of Fermi-LAT data above 2 GeV, with all-sky regions identified exhibiting significant spatial and temporal variability, including one emission at the Veil Nebula that is notably large and energetic.
