This study explores the potential of using the Pan-STARRS1 survey data to identify binary asteroids. A key aspect of the Pan-STARRS1 survey that makes it suitable for this purpose is its ability to accurately measure the positions of objects in the sky with high precision. A new method is developed to analyze the light curves of asteroids, taking into account their individual characteristics and the unique measurement patterns of the survey. This method was applied to 4440 main belt asteroids, resulting in the identification of 14 candidates for binary systems. These candidates have estimated periods of binary rotation ranging from 1.6 to 124 days. A more in-depth analysis of measuring light curves through imaging surveys is also presented as a valuable contribution of this study.

This study introduces a regression model that combines nonlinear network-related components with linear external variables and establishes a method for assessing the model's parameters and standard errors. Our estimation technique combines network analysis and regularization techniques to handle endogeneity, and yields standard errors that account for both network-based and extraneous sources of confusion, with varying rates of data growth. We also apply the model to online peer influence, finding strong evidence of peer effects in YouTube viewing patterns and precise assessments of the magnitude of those effects.

This study explores a novel interpretation of the product rule for the Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional integral and derivative. We establish a specific formulation of the product rule for the Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional integral, then use this to create a corresponding version for the variable-order Caputo-Feller initial value problem. Furthermore, there is no similar work on proving the product rule for the Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional integral, or on solving the variable-order Caputo-Feller initial value problem.

This work presents an original approach to a Theory-of-Mind (ToM) inquiry in Dungeons and Dragons, utilizing artificial intelligence. Our methodology encompasses the development of an AI Dungeon Master (DM) capable of guiding a D&D game, employing a ToM-based framework to manage multiple concurrent characters. Furthermore, we introduce a more sophisticated AI player that learns to engage in D&D gameplay, leveraging a reward system derived from the DM's feedback. As a means of evaluating our methodology, we conduct a comprehensive ToM-based D&D experiment involving both character interactions and strategic decision-making. Our findings reveal that our AI DM successfully guides a D&D game and our AI player exhibits improved ToM reasoning and strategic planning when guided by the DM's feedback.

The intricate three-dimensional structures of proteins determine their functionality, and while local interactions shape their two-dimensional sequences and three-dimensional configurations, forces arising from the three-dimensional space can lead to complex structures, including knots. Research has focused primarily on representing the chain of monomers locally to explain the three-dimensional structure, but exploring non-local patterns may provide additional insights. In this study, a method is developed to identify the chain arrangement from various possible configurations using topological and geometric criteria, and a technique is applied to examine the spatial patterns of knotted proteins, revealing that most of these proteins contain small, dense regions with a high degree of $\alpha$-helical structure that correspond to the knot's core position in the chain arrangement.

We establish a homomorphism of infinite index from the symplectic mapping class group of the blowup of a torus at a single point into the symplectic mapping class group of the original torus. Additionally, this index is proven to be maximal with respect to its reciprocal being an integer. This finding implies that no nontrivial representations of certain infinite subgroups of the symplectic mapping class group of the blowup of a torus can be realized.

A re-examination of the Nambu-Goldstone theorem within the framework of Quantum Field Theory is undertaken in this paper, with a focus on both its standard and both types of unconventional scenarios. A thorough exploration of the theorem's underlying principles is undertaken in the context of a general non-Abelian gauge theory with spontaneous symmetry breaking. Notable examples of spontaneous symmetry breaking in non-Abelian gauge theories are also examined, including SU(2) Higgs model, Yang-Mills-Higgs model, and the Standard Model. An examination of the mechanism behind the acquisition of mass by gauge bosons in the Standard Model is undertaken and the mechanism of the generation of mass for quarks and leptons is also discussed. The relationship between the number of quark and lepton generations and the structure of the generation mixing matrix is also explored. The linear response function formalism is shown to be a useful tool in the analysis of the number of massless Goldstone bosons in non-linearly realized symmetry breaking scenarios. The relevance of the non-relativistic quantum field theory is also discussed.

To improve how machines comprehend language, counterfactual examples are a valuable tool. While previous research has highlighted the significance of textual explanations in counterfactuals, previous studies have treated words as isolated components, neglecting the fact that language consists of meaningful phrases and structures. This study investigates whether neural network architectures can identify phrasal counterfactuals - minimal textual alterations to words within specific phrases that result in contrasting outcomes. Our analysis of 14 pre-trained language models reveals that these models are capable of recognizing phrasal counterfactuals, and even generating their own. Furthermore, we provide actionable advice for utilizing and creating phrasal counterfactuals effectively. To support our findings, we've made an extended paper available at https://github.com/rodrigoaguiar/disco.

The unique properties of Heusler semiconductors can be significantly improved through epitaxial graphene interfaces, yet this method requires precise control over van der Waals and remote or pinhole remote epitaxy. Researchers have discovered that the balance between these three forms of remote, pinhole, and van der Waals remote epitaxy in Heusler films grown on graphene and sapphire can be influenced by adjusting the substrate temperature. By fine-tuning the substrate temperature, the epitaxy type transitions from van der Waals to remote or pinhole remote and eventually to direct remote, pinhole, and van der Waals remote epitaxy. The transition temperatures for each form of epitaxy are determined through a combination of Raman spectroscopy, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and X-ray diffraction. Ultimately, the researchers achieved the equilibrium between the three forms of remote, pinhole, and van der Waals epitaxy in a specific Heusler film at a substrate temperature of 500°C. The resulting Mn$_3$Pt$_2$Sn$_4$ film exhibits a high-quality crystalline structure, high carrier mobility, and a high Curie temperature, indicating its potential for the development of spintronic devices.

For a prime number $p$, we examine $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes, which are codes constructed from the direct sum of $ \mathbb{Z}_p^n \oplus \mathbb{Z}_{p^2}^m $. We focus on the concept of the dimension of these codes over the direct sum, mirroring the approach used in $\mathbb{Z}_{p^k}$-linear codes. A code is classified as $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear if and only if it has a specific property known as a $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}}$-free basis. The set of all $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}}$-linear codes with a constant $p$ forms a family that can be parameterized. The collection of codes with a defined distance threshold also forms a code, specifically an ideal within the aforementioned family. Furthermore, we analyze the components of the local cohomology of the ideal defining the set of all $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}}$-free codes.

Supervised models trained on single positive labels for one task often excel at that task but struggle when faced with multiple simultaneous labels. This issue arises because single labels can represent either a single label or the union of multiple labels, leading models to learn the union of labels instead of all labels individually. This paper investigates the model's difficulty in handling simultaneous labels, proposing two methods to create multi-label examples from single positive data. Firstly, we present a search-based approach to generate simultaneous label instances, which can be applied to any dataset. Secondly, we introduce a probabilistic approach specifically for side information tasks, leveraging auxiliary information to manipulate single positive instances. Moreover, we develop a novel evaluation framework to assess both the difficulty of multi-label instances and the effectiveness of our synthesis methods. Through rigorous experiments, we demonstrate that models trained on multi-label instances achieve better performance compared to those trained solely on single positive data across various tasks.

The concept of a free functor was originally introduced in 1965 by Barr and Wells, with a significant application demonstrated in 1990 by Leinster. Since then, research has expanded to investigate various characteristics of free functors and their contrasting properties. Building upon these findings, this research aims to develop a framework for constructing a "free-on-somes" theory of linear functors and doctine morphines, and a separate "some-somes" theory of monoidal functors and natural transformations. The paper then seeks to demonstrate a connection between these theories, and a combination with the leinster free functor.

High-energy gamma-rays from galaxies have been observed for quite some time, but the source of gamma-rays from nearby galaxies with significant magnetic fields and visible emissions across the spectrum remains unclear. We propose that magnetic fields trapped by the galaxies' dynamics within a magnetized, massive disk could explain gamma-ray emissions from nearby galaxies. As long as the magnetic field strength exceeds a certain threshold and the amount of the field captured remains stable, the magnetic energy released as the field accumulates can be sufficient to account for the observed gamma-ray emissions. The energy that the captured magnetic field can release matches the energy required to produce gamma-rays in several galaxies, including M100, NGC 4594, NGC 3500B, and NGC 7603. Observations suggest that the structure of these galaxies' central regions, characterized by a dense bow-shaped pattern, matches the predicted distribution of the magnetic field captured in their disks.

This research heart sound categorization system is divided into two main categories: stethoscope conditions with added noise and healthy vs diseased hearts. The study uses a deep learning approach to automatically create features from sound signals using a 3D convolutional neural network (CNN). It explores two different noise types - uniform and Leaky noise - and compares the results with existing methods. The research also employs CNN to filter sound signals and reduce both types of noise. The model is trained to split sound data into two classes and re-records sounds with varying noise levels and playback speeds. The results show that the proposed method is more effective than traditional techniques in noisy environments, and the model is able to accurately classify hearts with a high F1 score.

The rapid growth of cloud computing and wearable technology has led to an increase in remote medical consultations and diagnoses. However, achieving high-quality diagnoses requires large datasets, which are difficult to gather due to patient privacy concerns. Federated learning offers a promising solution for training machine models in a decentralized environment, enabling data to remain on local devices while being used to train a shared model. Nevertheless, federated learning encounters difficulties when data across devices is not consistent. Our research focuses on developing a wearable medical diagnosis system that utilizes a more advanced framework than standard federated learning. This framework combines elements of transfer learning and federated learning to facilitate cross-device data heterogeneity. Federated transfer learning enables a model to be effectively deployed on wearable devices with varying data distributions by transferring a pre-trained model to a server and aggregating updates. In this framework, the server plays a crucial role as a virtual data aggregator, serving as a common reference point for model updates. Our proposed FedHealth framework has been evaluated on a real-world blood glucose dataset, and the results show that it outperforms existing methods in terms of wearable medical diagnosis performance.

This note explores recent advancements in portfolio theory, moving beyond traditional models that focus primarily on mean and variance, to include approaches centered on higher statistical moments.  The discussion examines how utilizing these higher moments can provide beneficial insights, particularly in terms of portfolio risk management during extreme market events. Additionally, various methods for estimating and modeling these higher orders, as well as relevant applications and limitations, are reviewed.

The sPCR2 Automated Software Visualization Platform combines previous features 
of the sPCR project, which merged Embyrd's sledgehammer and CProVer, two 
state-of-the-art automated theorem solvers. Now, sPCR2 integrates recent 
advancements from both projects it succeeded. It incorporates updated 
interfaces for sledgehammer and CProVer, improving compatibility and 
connectivity, as well as combining the libraries and functionalities of the 
sledgehammer and CProVer projects to streamline their combined capabilities.

Consider a game involving two players and three options, where the players take turns modifying one of the components of a state consisting of a point in space, a piece of information, and the cost incurred so far. These costs can change over time in a way that records all previous costs, and their nature is such that they don't increase. After the information component is modified for the final time, the player whose turn it is to act must pay the cost incurred and take the resulting value. This value is determined by maximizing the pay-off given the current cost incurred, or minimizing it given the opposing player trying to take advantage of this situation. This scenario is known as a toggle control problem with varying costs. We will take the step of defining the value function associated with this problem, and then investigate its property of changing in a stepwise manner in its cost incurred dimension. Ultimately, our research will culminate in the proof of this property.

The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has recently observed the production of top quarks and anti-top quarks via the strong force. Theoretical models involving new scalar particles, specifically a pair of scalar color-triplet fields, could potentially explain this observation. One of these scalar particles interacts with third-generation quarks while the other interacts with the second and third generations. A pair of these scalar particles could lead to the formation of a specific final state involving two top quarks and two bottom quarks, along with additional energy. An analysis of the LHC data at 13 TeV with a certain amount of collected information did not find evidence for these scalar particles, setting new limits on the parameters of the theoretical model.

A study of star-forming galaxies reveals that most molecules exist in a state that isn't fully thermally energized, and researchers are now examining the implications of this discovery. If these molecules are indeed in a subthermally excited state, it indicates a high density of molecular gas and low levels of infrared radiation. This environment is highly suitable for the formation of stars, and researchers are exploring ways to detect and analyze it. The study also proposes a new, more accurate method for calculating the star-formation potential of galaxies based on their carbon monoxide emissions. This revised approach is significantly more sensitive than the current standard method. The study emphasizes the importance of considering non-thermally excited molecules and calls for the development of more precise models to better understand and predict the formation of stars in galaxies.

Given the challenge of a newsvendor in a retail setting, where they must select a new stock arrangement $\kappa$ that optimizes their profits based on the historical purchase patterns of a customer, we analyze the underlying structure of the Hamming distance to identify and solve a specific problem known as the "series reconstruction problem." This involves finding a binary or multi-binary string of a specific length to minimize the total distance to a set of existing strings of different lengths, each weighted accordingly. We establish the difficulty of this problem in both its binary and multi-binary forms, then develop an efficient algorithm to address it, and further, an optimized version of this solution that limits the maximum string length to three times the longest original string. Additionally, we create a heuristic method to effectively manage instances where the string lengths are considerably larger. Our computational experiments showcase an impactful and limited strategy to address more intricate, real-life scenarios.

Researchers are investigating how the shape of pulsars' orbits influences the computational efficiency and feasibility of searching for specific non-spherical gravitational wave signals within data from pulsar timing arrays. By simulating a particular pulsar timing array correlation dataset based on the PPTA, they evaluated various approaches to model the precision with which each pulsar's elliptical shape parameters are estimated. This led to the development of two methods to estimate the confidence intervals for these parameters and their corresponding computational requirements. The results reveal that most timing models lead to significantly wider confidence intervals when elliptical shape parameters are estimated, and that this inaccuracy is notably affected by whether or not data is being actively analyzed. Although many timing models lead to extremely wide intervals for these parameters, the authors found that models including the Damodardas-Hughlling template and the AINS template achieve more manageable levels of inaccuracy. In contrast, models like the TaylorD2 and the PostNewtonian-precise tempo models lead to extremely wide intervals for these parameters, making the inclusion of these parameters unnecessary for most search methods. In fact, the latter two models may lead to significant misinterpretations of the data being analyzed.

We establish that in ASEP, the velocity process generated by a particular initial condition converges, in the limit of a large number of particles, to a stochastic process with non-degenerate Brownian increments and specified mean and variance. This has the potential to facilitate new applications of the CLT and related phenomena in the ASEP context.

Comprehensive epidemic modeling is crucial for effectively managing outbreaks and developing vaccines. Current models fall into two categories: those derived from fundamental principles, including the transmission of viruses and population interactions, and those based on statistical patterns observed in outbreak data. Although each type of model offers unique benefits, integrating both approaches provides a more powerful tool for understanding epidemics. This combined framework is especially valuable in light of the lessons learned from the COVID-19 pandemic.

Laser-induced three-body recombination enables the conversion of spinor atoms into molecules with a specific spin configuration. This research explores the conditions under which molecules made of Rb-87 can be created from Rb-87 molecules in an extremely low temperature environment. A theoretical model has been developed to predict the dynamic interplay between Rb-87 atoms, Rb-87 molecules in different spin states, and Rb-87 dimers made of two electrons. The results indicate that a high concentration of molecules in the desired spin state can be achieved by adjusting the frequency of an external field that modifies molecular bonds, and this state may have significant applications in precise measurements and stable molecule creation.

A next-generation storage solution called DNA has the potential to provide high-density and low-cost data storage. Despite its advantages, DNA storage still lags behind conventional storage in data management tasks, particularly in organizing file systems and updating files. This study presents two novel methods to address these challenges: a hierarchical FTL (File Transfer Layer) based on "DNA files" and a data refresh protocol called CRC-REX. The proposed CRC-REX method combines error correction codes with a randomized exchange process to prevent errors and maintain data integrity over time. Experimental results show that the hierarchical approach called DNA-FRT can efficiently manage data organization and minimize the costs associated with sequencing and synthesis. Additionally, the CRC-REX method outperforms existing protocols in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

Our novel hybrid approach seamlessly integrates the discrete exterior algebra (DEA) method for accurately representing the shallow water equations with a neural network (NN) to obtain numerical solutions. This innovation eliminates the requirement for traditional numerical solvers and paves the wayP for obtaining precise solutions to the shallow water equations in a highly efficient manner. By leveraging the topological consistency and numerical stability of the DEA-discrete shallow water equations, our NN-based solver guarantees mass conservation and enhanced numerical stability. Our results demonstrate the NN-based solver's remarkable speed, outperforming the DEA-discrete numerical method by two orders of magnitude in selected test cases. This approach provides a significant breakthrough in efficiently solving complex fluid dynamics problems and highlights the potential of deep learning techniques in scientific computations.

HDR photography combines multiple photos taken at different exposure levels to produce an image with an expanded dynamic range. A common issue with this technique is that it may introduce visible artifacts due to the inconsistent dynamic ranges of current camera sensors across different exposures. A mobile device's dynamic range is limited, and a common image processing technique, HDR fusion, relies on algorithms to select the best details from each photo. Our research explores an automatic exposure selection technique that determines the optimal exposures to capture on your mobile device, a new standard dHR fusion algorithm to combine the images, and an efficient real-time implementation on mobile devices. Our technique leverages a logarithmic model of perceived brightness to automatically set exposure levels, fuses images using the corresponding parts of the exposure range, and utilizes deep learning to train a controller that selects images based on the target scene's HR requirements. The resulting system provides a user-friendly and seamless HDR photography experience on mobile devices.

As deep neural networks become integral in high-stakes applications, the need to both regulate their underlying causal structures and enhance their ceteris paribus explanatory power is increasingly critical. This study introduces two significant advancements: first, a definition of causal neural network causality that extends beyond standard input-based explanations, and a corresponding optimization method to modify a trained network so that its altered structure accurately reflects desired causal properties; second, the development of flexible explanation frameworks that generalize from the current dataset, utilizing tailored interventions, and an efficient algorithm to determine the necessary network modifications to achieve a desired causal relationship, generalizing beyond the initial data, and to a specific instance. These ideas are put into practice through adaptations of popular neural network explanations, demonstrating the proposed approach's effectiveness through numerical and real-world case studies, along with a comparison of current causal explanation methods and an outline of future research directions.

This note introduces a new concept, the $r$-b-principle, which encompasses the b-principle as a specific case when the parameter $r$ equals one. Additionally, we demonstrate how $r$-mapping class group actions influence the $r$-b-principle. According to our findings, given any number $r$ that is greater than or equal to one, either the structure of the mapping class group alters the possibility of achieving the b-type for a given pair of manifolds in the case of $r$-links, or it does not at all. Moreover, the $r$-Mumford conjecture is proposed as a way to generalize the original Mumford conjecture by replacing $r$-character with character in its statement.

In this study, we compare the efficiency of three multilevel preconditioners, specifically FAS, geometric multigrid (GMG), and geometric preconditioned multigrid (GMP), in solving the non-linear equations that arise in cardiac mechanics simulations at a tissue level. To make an accurate comparison, we developed a comprehensive, open-source, and customizable simulation framework using Python and C++. Through this framework, we conducted a comprehensive, large-scale benchmark covering various physiological scenarios, including healthy and diseased conditions, as well as simple geometric models, over multiple time resolution levels. To ensure our results are applicable to a wider range of applications, we also integrated a highly scalable multilevel solver into our framework. Our benchmark reveals that for most models and time levels, the GMP method outperforms both the FAS and GMG methods. However, for high-resolution simulations involving realistic models of atrial mechanics at a tissue level, the MUPPET2 algorithm provides the best performance. Additionally, we found that for some lower-resolution simulations, the multilevel solver offers comparable or even superior performance to the best-performing multilevel method. All our benchmark data has been made publicly available to facilitate further research in this field.

The diffusion of particles through media with varying permeability can exhibit
non-Gaussian behavior, characterized by the cumulative diffusion coefficient, which
is non-linear. This study focuses on the 1D normal diffusion through non-Gaussian
random fields, specifically power-law distributions, and investigates non-
nonlinear relationships between non-averaged and averaged diffusion coefficients.
By conducting numerical simulations and theoretical calculations using renormalized
operators, we analyzed non-ergodic non-linear diffusion in time-reversible systems
and found that the non-linear connection between diffusion coefficients remains
consistent across different power-law distributions. This research highlights
how non-linear non-ergodic diffusion can be understood through cumulative
permeability distributions and emphasizes the significance of non-linear
relationships between non-averaged and averaged diffusion coefficients in
non-Gaussian random fields.

A comprehensive mathematical framework has been developed to analyze and understand the spatial distribution patterns of photons in optical components such as resonators and waveguides, taking into account both linear and Kerr nonlinear effects. This theory is applicable to a wide range of photonic structures, spanning from two-dimensional systems to those with complicated three-dimensional configurations. Within this framework, the spatial distributions of photons are broken down into a set of fundamental components that adhere to a set of specific rules that describe how they interact with one another and external fields. This set of components is found to be identical to a well-known collection of mathematical functions known as vector holographic functions. As a result, the often-complex and intractable interactions and effects observed in optical components can be significantly simplified and understood. This simplified view is demonstrated through a range of optical components, including a microresonator with a three-dimensional configuration, and the associated patterns of these components are visually represented in a set of detailed figures.

A primary goal in fluid dynamics research is visually analyzing complex turbulent flows, yet high-resolution velocity field visualizations are often inaccessible due to limited experimental velocity field data, typically containing small-scale turbulent fluctuations. In contrast, high-Reynolds number flows, easier to visually analyze due to their longer visualization streaks, often exceed 100,000, present challenging safety risks at required speeds. In this study, a super-resolution restoration technique based on a generative adversarial network was employed to recover high-Reynolds number velocity fields from low-Reynolds number velocity fields. A critical challenge in this task is matching the statistical characteristics of stochastic small-scale velocity streaks. To address this, a carefully designed generator and adversarial loss function were developed to enhance the naturalistic reconstruction of small-scale features. Experimental results demonstrate the effective super-resolution restoration capability of the proposed method. Furthermore, the restoration of velocity streaks visualizations was successfully achieved in both straight and curved channels at high Reynolds numbers based on generated velocity fields and validated through velocity streak distribution analysis.

Next-generation intelligent systems must excel in unpredictable, changing environments where fundamental shifts occur unexpectedly. To advance such learning capabilities, a lifelong approach to reinforcement learning has emerged, focusing on prioritizing challenging learning opportunities and developing efficient multi-task algorithms. Despite its potential, the advancement of lifelong reinforcement learning lags behind supervised learning in terms of evaluation standards and benchmarks. To address this shortfall, we present Lifelong Explorer, a cutting-edge evaluation platform that encompasses ten distinct tasks spanning various complexities and time periods, seamlessly convertible to lifelong learning settings. This environment offers diverse generalization scenarios, including real-world applications with 10 real-world datasets, and is equipped with modern evaluation tools, such as adaptive benchmarking and standardized generalization testing. We also provide a thorough exploration of available data, algorithms, and evaluation methods to facilitate the development of lifelong learning strategies. To demonstrate the possibilities of this platform, we include examples of lifelong settings, generalization challenges, and a multi-task reinforcement learning algorithm. We invite the broader research community to utilize this comprehensive evaluation environment to push the boundaries of multi-task and lifelong reinforcement learning. Lifelong Explorer's open-source code and documentation are accessible at https://github.com/GoogleResearch/L2Explorer.

Human operators are an invaluable component in the realm of process management, yet they are often sidelined in process management systems. These systems frequently neglect to capitalize on their potential for both learning and exploration. This study introduces a novel Approach and Algorithm for extracting knowledge from and experimenting with a single user within a declarative process system. The process system is designed to seamlessly integrate exploration and learning aspects, drawing on the concept of Utility Estimation through Bayes' UCB criterion. The proposed method enables processes to be analyzed in terms of data flows, facilitating learning from instances and enabling experimentation by limiting possible actions to those that could yield valuable outcomes. The efficacy of the proposed Approach and Algorithm is validated through a variety of artificial and real-world process cases, demonstrating its ability to exploit prior knowledge, encourage learning, and account for exploration in order to achieve its objectives.

This paper provides an overview of compactification methods for moduli spaces, examining both their geometric foundations and algebraic constructs. The discussion highlights various compactification techniques, including their applications to the study of function fields and geometric invariant theory.

The relationship between star formation rates (SFR) and total stellar mass experiences a "quenching turn" for massive galaxies, yet it's unclear what causes this specific behavior in galaxies with over 10^11 solar masses. We believe bulge growth is a key factor in driving this "quenching turn". By breaking down our sample into bulge-dominated and disk-dominated galaxies, we found that the SFR-stellar mass curve for bulge-dominated galaxies exhibits an earlier turnover compared to disk-dominated galaxies. We propose a two-step process to explain why bulge-dominated galaxies experience an earlier shift towards the "quenching sequence": first, bulge growth itself is linked to quenching in massive galaxies through various mechanisms, and then, disk-dominated galaxies naturally transition to bulge-dominated galaxies as their masses increase. Our findings provide a consistent framework to explain the varying points where different galaxy types transition to the "quenching sequence" and also account for the delayed quenching turn observed in some previous studies.

This sentiment classification model spans five languages, English, French, German, Italian, and Portuguese, across four distinct domains: social media, news, movie reviews, and Amazon reviews. It achieves success in single-domain sentiment classification across these languages and provides an example of data-sequence learning.

This research focuses on creating a method to identify ICU patients with the COVID-19 disease based solely on X-ray images. The COVID-19 X-ray dataset used in this study is the one from Reference 1. It contains 1,385 images labeled for pneumonia, PND, and normal conditions. The proposed algorithm combines hand-crafted features with a ResNet-50 deep learning model. It achieves higher accuracy than previous methods in identifying whether a patient requires intensive care, with the proposed algorithm's mean accuracy, macro F1 score, and AUC values being 0.91, 0.88, and 0.91, respectively. The research also highlights the critical role of texture analysis in differentiating healthy lungs from those affected by COVID-19.

We've established that a simplicial bundle over a simplicial group S, S → A, consistently maps to a simplicial group through the functor δ, resulting in the relationship δS → δA. This implication holds true for all simplicial bundles.

This work focuses on addressing a significant issue in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD) where a large number of false relationships are predicted due to objects being misidentified as they overlap in an image. Our research reveals that over 60% of predicted relationships stem from this issue, resulting in low recall of valid relationships and an abundance of false positives. To tackle this problem, we introduce a novel framework called Spatially-Aware Post Filter (SAPF) that leverages the 3D geometry of scene elements to eliminate false predictions. Specifically, we utilize the spatial configuration of a scene to determine the plausibility of a relationship based on the distance and orientation between two objects in 3D space. Our proposed method is straightforward to implement and does not require any modifications to existing VRD models. Through comprehensive experiments on the Visual Relational Navigation (VRN) and Visual Genome (VG) datasets, we found that our approach significantly reduces the number of false predictions, enhances the model's navigation accuracy, and increases the detection of valid relationships. Our results indicate an improvement of 11.5 points in mean intersection over union (mIOU) of predicted relationships, an 18.3 points decrease in false positives per image, and an 11.1 points increase in the number of detected relationships on the VG dataset. Our code is available at https://github.com/ChengShi1999/SAPF.

We've used deep observations from the Hubble and XMM-Newton telescopes to examine a galaxy, DWGN 261, which is at a distance of 11.16 gigaparsecs from Earth. This galaxy exists in a rich cluster of galaxies and is characterized by an enormous, one-sided stellar disk, along with a smaller group of older stars in the center. By analyzing the distribution of older stars and young, massive stars, we found that the galaxy's bulge is small and spherical, while the massive stars are primarily located in spiral arms and a small group in the center. We've created a 3D model of the galaxy's star groups and found that the older, massive, and low-mass stars share the same physical location, suggesting they were created from the same gas cloud. We've also determined that the galaxy's one-sided nature is due to a group of smaller galaxies merging, which brought new, rotating gas clouds that formed the massive, one-sided disk and the small, spherical bulge through internal forces, rather than by bringing older stars from other galaxies. This internal process of bulge creation is a common occurrence in galaxy clusters and is an important factor to consider in future galaxy formation theories.

On November 7, 2004, a massive solar flare occurred at location 254 degrees, classified as X1.8, and led to several space weather effects. This event was associated with type II and III radio bursts, an intense geomagnetic storm of G5 rating, and a rare observation of ground-level solar neutrons. Notably, during this flare, two distinct solar events resulting in solar proton components were observed. The first, a short-duration high energy proton event with peak fluxes exceeding 3000 p/(s cm2 sr MeV) at 1.5 MeV, and the second, a long-duration low energy proton event with maximum intensity around 10 hours post-solar onset, were both identified. Both events were attributed to multiple coronal current sheets and magnetic reconnection processes. The interaction of these two events resulted in significant solar energy release, the generation of type II solar radio bursts, and a substantial flux of Earth-directed solar neutrons.

The discovery of PDS 70 protoplanet located beyond the disk's break, which is suspected to result from angular momentum transfer obstacles, has intriguing implications. Some researchers speculate that if the planet gained its angular momentum through interactions with the disk, it might indicate that the planet is still in the process of forming. However, we contend that even the most massive young planets can easily overcome angular momentum transfer barriers at specific mass ratios, making a comparison with disk observations straightforward. As a result, finding the PDS 70 protoplanet within a gas disk is a remarkable achievement, but it does not necessarily represent a groundbreaking development in planet formation.

The rapid proliferation of social media has given false news a significant advantage in its spread, posing a serious threat to public safety and stability.  Effective methods for detecting false news have become a crucial area of research.  Traditional approaches often rely on manually crafted features, while contemporary techniques utilize automatic features from vast amounts of data to identify news authenticity.  However, these models struggle to generalize when applied to new domains or when news is too recent for their training datasets.  Although few-shot learning has shown promise in addressing this challenge, the incorporation of both text and image data for false news detection remains largely unexplored.  Current models for few-shot news detection also fail to capture the relationship between media and can lead to misleading associations in detecting false news.  In response to these challenges, we present a novel emergent few-shot false news detection framework, called MM-MNPP, which leverages a K-way few-shot setting and utilizes a multimodal emergent network process to detect false news across text and image data.  By employing a hard negative sample selection mechanism and a pseudo-triplet loss function, our model captures the relationship between media and enhances generalization ability.  Experiments conducted on two widely used datasets demonstrate the superiority of our approach over state-of-the-art baselines in detecting false news in emerging domains.

The research paper delves into the conveyance equation under periodic conditions, considering source and velocity fields that repeat at a given period. It highlights recent findings regarding the ANSIs in periodic flow optimization. Additionally, it presents new evidence conveying the usefulness of ANSIs in predicting the frequency of ANSIs based on the interaction of velocity and vorticity fields. It is demonstrated that three distinct sides of the ANSIs' nature - historical, electrical, and fluid mechanical - are equally significant in their original contexts.

A new construction method for polyphase Golay complementary sets (PACS) is presented, specifically for periodic functions drawn from a set of $2n$ such functions with a periodicity of $n$. The construction utilizes PACS of length $n$ and a single PACS of length $2$, or alternatively, PACS of lengths $n$ and $m$ where $n$ is less than $m$ and both are integers. The construction is backed by mathematical proof and examples, including the construction of a 140-length PACS from 70-length PACS and a 268-length PACS from a 100-length PACS and a 6-length PACS, as well as the 12-length PACS from Buss and Stark's construction, which can be used to create infinite PACS sets based on any prime $p$ where $p$ congruent to $1$ (mod 12). The construction also enables the creation of orthogonal primaries with Pacific-ACL properties.

Silicon's unique valley structure in its $k$-space contributes to various quantum phenomena and technological advancements.
In particular, the distinct behavior of electrons localized in individual valleys leads to interaction patterns that exhibit entanglement and energy exchange between the valleys, manifesting as phenomena like tunneling and interference.
This research reports on the first observation Valley interaction and spin transfer between Silicon's separated valleys for the first time.
By isolating electrons in a double double quantum dot and switching the valleys using an electric field, researchers were able to observe tunneling and interference patterns between the separated valleys, and used coupled double quantum dots to demonstrate trans-valley coupling-mediated spin transfer and phase-dependent interference patterns.
These discoveries demonstrate the potential of valley qubits and provide a basis for developing novel entanglement generation schemes and phase-controlled spin transfer mechanisms in Silicon-based technology.

The rapid expansion of complex systems research has been fueled by the abundance of multi-dimensional data, yet understanding the underlying dynamics that govern these systems remains a significant challenge. In this talk, I will discuss the difficulties in analyzing complex dynamics and present a new, simpler model based on a linear dynamical system, which can be effectively trained using a graph neural network framework. This approach has been successfully applied to a variety of complex systems, including the spread of diseases, the propagation of fake news on social media, and the behavior of financial markets.

Topological K-theory enumerates the number of ways to split a positive integer into smaller integers, each raised to a power of two. Can a similar enumerative property be established for other algebraic structures within algebraic K-theory? Specifically, how can we interpret the elements of $K_1(\mathbb{N})$ in terms of integers and their decomposition into smaller integers? Can we extend this perspective to understand $K_1$ of semisimple algebras formed by direct sums of matrix algebras over the real numbers, denoted as $A_n = \bigoplus_{i=1}^k M_{n_i}(\mathbb{R})$? Does a natural correspondence exist between the components of these algebras and a partition of an integer into smaller integers?

Deep learning techniques, particularly convolutional neural networks, have made considerable progress in medical image analysis.  However, acquiring adequate annotated data is often challenging due to the difficulty of annotating images accurately and ethically.  To address this challenge, researchers have turned to data augmentation methods, including generating synthetic lesions to augment healthy images.  The purpose of these synthetic lesions is to train disease detection models more effectively.  In this work, we propose an innovative approach to generate synthetic lesions using a progressive training strategy based on a 3D adaptive variational adversarial auto-encoder framework.  Our method allows for the precise manipulation of synthetic lesions' physical and geometric properties, allowing for easier evaluation of disease detection models with controlled variables.  Experimental results demonstrate that Models trained on synthetic lesions achieve better performance compared to those trained on data-augmented real lesions, with minimal performance loss of 2%.

A significant improvement to the GP 2 GenProlog-2 parser generator has been made, 
which is a tool for creating parsers in GenProlog. A second-generation GP 2 
compiler, developed by Kristian G. Kjoeller, takes GP 2 files as input and 
produces an updated GP 2 file as output, effectively serving as a text-based 
editor with GP 2 specific capabilities. In addition to modifying a GP 2 file, 
the compiler incorporates changes that improve the compatibility of the GenProlog-2 
system with the parser it generates. The updated system also benefits from 
correct handling of tag assignments, removal of unused temporary variables, and 
adjustments to temporary variable declarations.

Recent advancements in self-supervised learning, particularly in contrastive learning, have shown significant success in various tasks. This work delves into the underlying principles of contrastive learning by categorizing four distinct contrastive learning methods into three categories based on their source of information. A striking revelation emerges when examining the performance of a unified model that incorporates a specific contrastive learning component in conjunction with a modest BERT feature extractor, demonstrating notable enhancements in classification performance across seven different datasets. The experimental results highlight the value of certain contrastive learning models for extracting robust representations, thereby informing the design of more effective downstream applications.

In the study of finite simple group theory, a significant classification effort focuses on determining specific families and exceptional groups of $T$-quotient diagrams. A key property of these $T$-quotient diagrams is their "star" characteristic, which has been established for many groups, although a smaller number of potential candidates remain unconfirmed through extensive computational verification through Liebeck and Shalev's proposed $T$-quartet conjecture. A particular subclass of diagrams, referred to as "twisted" due to their unique construction, belongs to an infinite family of specific structures. This paper introduces an infinite family of "twisted" normal quotient diagrams of a particular class of groups, denoted as $G$, based on a semi-direct product of two groups, $C_p^n$ and $SL_2(q)$, where the parameters $n$ and $q$ adhere to the relation $n(q-1)=p-1$. This finding significantly broadens a previously established result by Asaad and Karpilovsky from 1991, which demonstrated the existence of specific $T$-quartet graphs for the same parameters. This work also rectifies a limitation of its own preceding study, which only established the existence of specific "twisted" $T$-quartet $diagrams$ for the $GL_n(q)$ general linear group through its own unique construction.

Working with high-dimensional nominal data is becoming increasingly common in a wide range of applications, yet effective methods for identifying relevant groups of variables within such data sets remain limited. To address this challenge, we developed an enhanted group lasso technique for nominal data that can be fine-tuned to select important variable groups for prediction or visualization purposes. We carefully analyzed the theoretical properties of this method and conducted an extensive examination using synthetic data and real-world data from six data sets, comparing our approach with other high-dimensional selection methods. Our results show that the enhanted group lasso accurately selects variable groups for prediction and visualization, often outperforming alternative methods. Furthermore, we made available both the package and an user guide demonstrating its usage.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved significant success in natural language processing tasks. However, these models often struggle with handling factual information due to their tendency to generate plausible but incorrect content in several domains, including knowledge-based question-answering, machine reading comprehension, and textual entailment. To address this challenge, various methods have been developed to refine the predictions of these models through training adjustments, prompt engineering, or parameter tuning. Unfortunately, these approaches have limitations, such as requiring extensive fine-tuning data, necessitating large amounts of training, or suffering from limited transferability. In contrast, our proposed approach, ABILITY, leverages structured information from external knowledge graphs through simple visualization generation based on natural language prompts, thereby improving the accuracy of model outputs without compromising their generalization capabilities. Notably, ABILITY demonstrates superior performance compared to other methods that utilize structured knowledge, such as BERT+KG and RAG, while also being more efficient in terms of time and computational resources. Refined versions of ABILITY further demonstrate enhanced performance while maintaining computational efficiency.

The rapid expansion of Augmented Reality (AR) applications necessitates a seamless integration of virtual elements into the real world, a task that relies heavily on accurate and high-quality 3D graphics. Line junctions, formed when map lines intersect, create watermarks in 2D representations and anti-aliased effects in 3D representations, which can detract from the user experience. To address this issue, an investigation was conducted to analyse the causes of watermarks and anti-aliasing effects and to develop an innovative spatial anti-aliasing method for line junctions. The proposed approach involves a three-step process: a pre-processing step to adjust line line junctions, a real-time processing step to modify line circle junctions, and a post-processing step to adjust line circle junctions. The results of this research indicate a significant improvement in visual quality and a minor increase in rendering time, providing a valuable reference for future developments in spatial anti-aliasing for both 2D and 3D graphics.

To enhance single-microphone speech for several simultaneous conversations, current models typically rely on multiple microphones and a speech recognition system to determine which speaker to improve based on their content. Although effective, this approach is constrained by the necessity of using a specific number of microphones and a reliance on an external system to guide the process. In this study, a unique single-microphone model is proposed that emulates a dual-path system, emulating both the structure and behavior of multiple microphones, thereby circumventing the necessity for a speech recognition system and allowing a single microphone to be used for simultaneous conversations. This model is capable of managing any number of speeches without the limitation of the number of microphones in use. Furthermore, it achieves superior performance in assessing a simultaneous conversation and determining the target speech to improve, outperforming existing approaches that rely on model-based or data-driven methods.

Two-fluid modeling holds potential for capturing atmospheric convection within a single column. By simulating fast-moving and slow-moving fluids within the same column, such a model can replicate the convection processes seen in the atmosphere. To achieve this, we developed a two-fluid model and tested it using the Rayleigh-Benard setup, replicating atmospheric convection within a solar atmosphere. The model accurately captured the transition from steady to oscillating convection patterns as the Rayleigh number increased. It also matched previous research on how heat transfer changes with the Rayleigh number and the influence of gas pressure. Notably, the model also took into account gas pressure effects absent in most model-based research. As it aligns with solar atmosphere conditions, the two-fluid model demonstrates its capability to simulate solar surface convection processes. However, verifying this requires precise thermal infrared observations of the solar surface. To move forward, we need to refine the model to a multi-fluid framework.

The concept of entanglement, which is a purely quantum phenomenon, becomes more complex when considering the origin of the particles involved. While particles produced through identical methods are commonly used in experiments to demonstrate the particle nature of quantum fields, particles found in nature are often uncoupled from one another and may exhibit distinct characteristics. In a recent study, the process of creating entanglement between two uncoupled particles in separate Jaynes-Cummings cavities was investigated for the first time. The particles in question were not the same type and were located in different spatial positions. The research demonstrated that a particle could become entangled with another through the exchange of virtual photons with the cavities, provided the Jaynes-Cummings interaction was within a specific range. The speed at which this process occurs and its duration were also explored in relation to interaction strength and the distinct properties of the particles involved. Furthermore, the research examined how the process would be affected by decoherence and the development of an entanglement generator using two independent Jaynes-Cummings cavities was discussed.

A Twitter user's emotional expression on social media platforms can be
positive, negative, or neutral. Determining their overall sentiment is an
emotional classification task with three categories. In this paper, we present an
emotional classification model for Twitter users that considers three emotional
states – happy, sad, or angry. We describe anemotional labeling approach
based on social media posts and present an Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)
network for predicting the emotional state of a user's profile. We tested our
approach using the 2013 and 2016 Emotion/Sentiment on Twitter Data (ESTD)
datasets and showed that our LSTM framework effectively predicts the three
emotional states of a user's profile.

Researchers have examined the connection between nonlinear charged black holes in anti-de Sitter space and the concept of shadow thermodynamics. A key finding reveals that the charge-to-mass ratio directly influences the connection between an black hole's Holographic surface and its squared effective charge, with a specific relationship emerging at a particular mass threshold. The research also uncovers that the mass and temperature of the black holes are directly proportional, while their squared effective charge and squared temperature are inversely related. Additionally, a link is established between the Holographic surface and the squared effective charge to the power of the temperature to the power of two, first in linear and then in non-linear scenarios. The surface of the black holes is found to be inversely proportional to the product of their temperature and their squared effective charge to the power of two. The researchers have plotted the above-mentioned relationships to provide a more in-depth understanding of the phenomena occurring.

Recent advances in optical sorting networks have incorporated angle-dependent reflection characteristics, leading to angle-based angular expansion and mutual interference patterns. Our research utilizes a specialized method to visualize these phenomena in optical 2D grating (ODG) tomograms. By leveraging 3D space characteristics, optical ODG tomograms can display increased angular ranges as a result of reflection characteristics, and adjacent spacers' differences can result in beginning of interference patterns, manifesting as angular compression or expansion. This interpretation is supported by mathematical analysis using the Radon transform.

In this work, forecasting user viewports in 360-degree travel videos is modeled, where predicted content helps anticipate where users will look and supports the development of improved user experience tools. A dataset was assembled and made available for research purposes, consisting of 47,745 predicted-user viewports and 36,600 three-second historical video clips, each clip being associated with a future three-second viewport in 3D space. A baseline approach was established and multiple machine learning techniques were evaluated to address this challenge effectively.

We develop a novel approach to construct an approximate global tensor network for a three-dimensional hypercubic lattice, focusing on the generator of a thermal state and the result of a unitary evolution. In both cases, the system's Hamiltonian undergoes a local thermalization or thermalizes within a specific region under a unitary operation. And the tensor network's peacocks indicate two key properties: the number of thermalization legs remains constant with temperature or the duration of evolution, and the network's entropy capacity remains limited, facilitating a balanced cost for both aspects. And the initial approach employs Fisher's phase trick to decompose two dimensions of the Hamiltonian into a series of Pauli Z operators and excitation states represented by hypercatalytic tensor structures. And the third dimension remains catalytic through a "peacock" structure, facilitating efficient simulation of the system's thermal and dynamic properties using a variational Monte Carlo method. And the results obtained using 3D hypercubic catalytic tensor network state demonstrate the method's efficiency and the potential for utilizing a 4D hypercubic version to simulate a 3D thermal lattice system with significant accuracy. And the cost of simulation remains relatively low, primarily due to the moderate number of hypercatalytic tensor structures involved.

Decoupling in probability theory can be simplified by understanding through scale-oriented approximations of a "restricted efficacy" decoupling technique. This basic decoupling technique is limited but useful, as it efficiently transforms a sum of random variables with a specific condition into one with comparable expected values. When combined with other established and newly developed scale-oriented approximations, this method is applicable to transform inequalities, such as decoupled Carbery-Wright ones, into their original forms.

The critical role of infrared renormalons in factorization theory is commonly illustrated through TMD PDFs associated with dipoles under high-energy conditions. By conducting an in-depth examination of the $x$-dependent Tglb gluon TMD PDF within the color dipole model, we explore the implications of a specific infrared renormalon, specifically the leading $1/x$ type. Our analysis uncovers that this effect is substantial and results in a significant enhancement of the gluo-ball component in the structure $F_2$ for proton deep virtual Compton scattering at the onset of the deep virtual region.

Two-dimensional crystal lattices composed of metallic structures exhibit geometric properties known as topological characteristics, which can lead to unique optical properties including topological photonic bands and robust photon transport that resists disruptions. The strength of this geometric interaction relies heavily on the specific orientation of the lattice in relation to an external reference frame, which complicates its implementation in applications. We present a novel approach using split-ring resonators to create lattice orientations with distinct topological properties, enabling a photonic catalyst with the ability to switchable photonic isolation and the transfer of geometry-independent topological lattice behavior. This breakthrough facilitates the development of integrated photonic circuits with a mix of conventional and unique lattice geometries, as well as a reference frame for geometric interaction based on the orientation of triatomic components.

Decision-making models are becoming essential in various domains, yet their effectiveness relies on adequate training data. In scenarios where training data is limited or unavailable, transferring knowledge from these models can significantly enhance the performance of simpler decision-making frameworks. This study focuses on transferring knowledge from a decision-based black-box framework, which makes predictions depending on input feature values, even when trained via deep learning methods. We investigate two novel black-box knowledge transfer approaches. The first approach, ZS-TestSet, generates decisions from the black-box framework using test set data, excluding any label information, before training an open-set decision tree. The second approach, ZS-Single, creates synthetic data points by feeding a single, ZS instance into the decision-based framework, and then trains the ZS DTree on these generated data. The results demonstrate that both knowledge transfer methods outperform training the ZS DTree alone and achieving the same level of performance as more complex, GBDT-based decision models. Additionally, when contrasted with another knowledge transfer method that uses ZS labels, both the ZS-TestSet and ZS-Single approaches yield comparable results.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L$ decay mode, both of which provide insights into $K^0_L$ hadronization. The branching fraction for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ is determined to be $(4.3\pm 0.5\pm 0.1\pm 0.2)\times 10^{-5}$, and the branching fraction for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L$ is $(10.0\pm 1.9\pm 0.4\pm 0.5)\times 10^{-5}$, with the uncertainties being statistical in nature and the second set being systematic in nature.

In the study of lattice theory, a significant concept is that of a distributive lattice of lattice congruences for Young's Symmetric Group, which is isomorphic to the lattice of submodules of a specific type of module, denoted as $\wedge YSR$, under the Specht module $YSR$. The $YSR$ module is part of a family of symmetric group modules that are characterized by having a composition of one. This paper provides a method for constructing the lattice of submodules of $\wedge YSR$ from partial information, which is based on the intrinsic structure of $YSR$ and its submodules. The construction method is demonstrated through the use of $S_7$ as an example, and the resulting lattice is made visually accessible through an extended diagram. Additionally, a new characterization of the rank 3 submodules of multiplicity zero in the $YSR$ module is discovered, which is defined by the property of being generated by minimal congruences corresponding to 2-segs, and which is in turn in a one-to-one relationship with the set of pairs of disjoint non-nested segments in the Dyck path of its associated semistandard Young tableau.

In this work, we consider a co-learning framework where an agent and a student observe and act independently in the same environment, with the goal of mastering a task given its individual prior knowledge, given access to an additional, potentially costly expert demonstration. We analyze twoCo-Sequential Partially Observable Learning (CO-PSL) and CO-Observation Learning (CO-SL)) problems, distinguishing whether the student can see the agent's actions or only sees the same state and rewards as the agent. We propose COQ learning algorithms that can achieve this across both PSL and SL settings, and demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods through theoretical performance guarantees and practical applications.

In this paper, we provide a metric definition that differentiates between PAC codes and traditional error correcting codes, establishing a foundation for further development. Building on this definition, we create a method to calculate the PAC weight, which encompasses and refines existing approaches, including Trevisan's original method and the high-weight metric introduced by Parvaresh and Rudra. This new calculation strategy is demonstrated through various existing and novel PAC codes, establishing PAC codes in a conventional metric framework and offering a clearer understanding of their relationship with conventional CRC codes. Additionally, we highlight the significance of the PAC high-weight property in enhancing Reed-Solomon code performance when used in iterative decoding frameworks.

Neural machine translation (NMT) currently relies on a network to directly map input translations to output distributions in an end-to-end manner. Although this approach has achieved significant performance, its training process assumes simple action spaces where network parameters are continuously adjusted. In reality, NMT components often have limited and discrete action spaces, such when using a vocabulary-based encoder or a fixed structure decoder. To address this issue, we investigate reinforcement learning (RL) with an extensive action space NMT model and discover that RL training can lead to notable improvements over traditional supervised learning NMT methods. To facilitate this, we develop a novel multi-task learning framework that allows the NMT model to excel across both continuous and limited action spaces. Our approach demonstrates that leveraging multiple action spaces benefits the NMT model, while also yielding significant gains over using only the largest action space. To validate these claims, we conducted comprehensive experiments on the NMT model, which showed that our proposed framework delivers tangible benefits.

In this study, we investigate the dynamics of a quantum bit in a non-equilibrium steady state, which is influenced by a time-varying magnetic field with a specific pattern. This approach enables the exploration of both Landau-Zener and Stokes interference phenomena using a single experiment. As the two phenomena interact, we observe a range of behaviors, from additive to oscillating and even additive patterns with a phase shift. This same framework can be applied to other areas of research.

We introduce a new category of set properties called p/q-identifiable, which stands as an expansion of properties such as id and m-id. A specific property within this category, 1/1-identifiable (equivalent to id), is demonstrated to be equivalent to the T1-identifiable property. The set of id properties forms a structured collection with defined relationships of inclusion. The article also explores id properties in the context of topological spaces and semitopological groups, providing proof that 1/1-identifiable spaces are necessarily id spaces, and thus spaces with the id topology. The set of all id properties forms an infinite collection that includes various well-known properties like T0, T1, T2, T2.5, T3, T3.5, T4, T4.5, and m-id spaces. The article further establishes the existence of specific relationships of 1/p-identifiable spaces, and offers an algorithm to generate a collection of spaces that help define the boundaries of these properties.

NoSQL databases, including MongoDB, are gaining popularity for their efficiency with large-scale data. MongoDB's flexibility and ease of use make it particularly appealing. However, the document-oriented structure of MongoDB presents challenges in ensuring data consistency and transactional integrity. In this study, we developed a tool called TIGER to automate the verification of transactional integrity in MongoDB. TIGER leverages the database execution log to efficiently check the consistency of transactions, minimizing performance impact. Our tests show that TIGER can detect incorrect transactions and demonstrate its ability to scale with large production databases, providing a reliable method for ensuring MongoDB's transactional reliability.

In 1983, Stanley proved the $e$-positivity of the chromatic symmetric function for graphs with a specific property, leading us to investigate the connection between these functions and the non-negative inverse of the Kostka matrix associated with a particular set of compositions. This exploration reveals that the inverse of this matrix consists of $e$-positive coefficients, except for a specific composition where the coefficient is instead $s$-positive. The $s$-positivity of the chromatic symmetric functions is also demonstrated, providing the first occurrence of $s$-positivity in this context. Furthermore, we provide a more comprehensive framework for understanding the relationship between the chromatic symmetric functions and the inverse of the Kostka matrix by introducing a new class of composition matrices, specifically those with the $s$-non-negativity property. This new class of matrices is explored in greater depth, yielding additional results, including the non-negative inverse of the composition matrix of compositions within an interval, an explicit formula for the inverse of the matrix of compositions of an arithmetic progression, and the connection between the inverse of the composition matrix of an arithmetic progression and the Catalan triangle.

The underlying structure of intricate networks significantly influences the formation of these networks and leads to various types of network connections that manifest in various fields, such as the natural world, societal interactions, and things manufactured by humans. The study of intricate, concealed geometric patterns within network structures is essential for a deeper understanding and exploitation of network dynamics. The present research focuses on revealing and concealing geometric patterns within intricate networks through the creation of triangular and pairwise magnetic interactions within triangular aluminum nanostructures, using aluminum-based Josephson circuits as a manufacturing platform. The research reveals the nature of these hidden geometric patterns and their influence on the dynamics of a type of intricate quantum network known as a spin glass, providing a method for controlling the nature of these patterns and their effects on the behavior of intricate quantum networks. The results obtained in this study offer the basis for the development of intricate quantum devices with advanced functionality.

A critical shift in our comprehension of solar influence on the inner solar system and planetary systems is made possible by the new data provided by the Parker Solar Probe, particularly in the inner solar system. The initial measurements of the inner heliosphere, taken by PSP's Plasma Science Experiment (SWEAP/PAS), reveal the solar wind's characteristics along its first three orbits. The solar wind's properties at the location of the first three PAS encounters show little variation, likely due to their occurrences within the same high-speed stream. The first two encounters took place within the same stream, whereas the third encounter happened in a different but similarly fast-moving sector about 180 degrees away in heliolatitude. The radial solar wind flow energy flux density was found to be nearly constant, with values between 4.0 and 4.6 PW, as expected from the conservation of energy. The variations observed in the inner heliosphere are primarily the result of magnetic fluctuations in the solar wind streams, rather than changes in the properties of the plasma. The detailed characteristics of the solar wind streams, which are crucial for the safety of the spacecraft and the interpretation of the data, are predicted with high accuracy. The accuracy of the stream boundary forecasts made for the first three encounters is confirmed by the actual observations. The solar wind data obtained by PAS serves as a benchmark for the characteristics of the solar wind in the inner heliosphere, even in the absence of other instruments in the inner solar system.
